bio.en: Jules Walter is a product leader at YouTube who was Slack's first growth PM and later led its monetization and mobile teams, and co-founded nonprofits expanding diversity in tech.
bio.zh: 朱尔斯·沃尔特（Jules Walter）是 YouTube 的产品负责人，曾是 Slack 的第一位增长产品经理，后来领导其变现与移动团队，并联合创办了推动科技行业多样性的非营利组织。

summary.en: Jules emphasizes treating feedback as a gift by genuinely thanking people and internalizing it, even when it stings. He shares lessons on building product sense, running growth at Slack, and creating pathways for underrepresented product managers. The conversation is full of practical advice for early-career PMs on learning faster and seeking honest feedback.
summary.zh: 朱尔斯强调要把反馈当作礼物——真诚道谢并内化吸收，哪怕它让人难受。他分享了在 Slack 做增长的经验、培养产品感的体会，以及为代表性不足的产品经理创造机会的故事。本期充满对早期产品经理如何更快学习、主动寻求真实反馈的实用建议。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: If you give me feedback, I'll be like, "Hey, thank you so much. This is super helpful," because people are like, "Oh, he actually likes the feedback." Now, inside my heart might be melting. I'm like, "Oh, I thought I got better at this." You know what I mean?
turns.zh: 要是你给我反馈，我会说：“嘿，太感谢你了。这对我超级有帮助。”因为别人会觉得：“哇，他居然真的喜欢这种反馈。” 其实我心里可能已经乐开花了。我会想：“哦，我还以为自己已经做得不错了。” 你懂我的意思吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: But externally, I'm like, "Hey, thank you," and I mean it. I think that's the key that most people don't focus on. And if you get more feedback, then you'll just get better at the things.
turns.zh: 但表面上，我还是会说：“嘿，多谢啦，”而且我是真心的。我觉得这才是大多数人忽略的关键。只要多接受反馈，你就能在这些事情上做得越来越好。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Hey, Lenny. Thanks for having me. I'm really excited.

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah, same here.
turns.zh: 是啊，我也是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's just start with a quick overview of your background. Could you share some of the wonderful places you've worked, some of the wonderful projects you've worked on, and then just a bit about what you're working on today?
turns.zh: 首先，让我们快速回顾一下你的背景。能否分享一些你曾工作过的优秀公司、参与过的精彩项目，以及你目前的工作内容？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah, happy to. Some quick background, grew up in Haiti, studied computer science in college, went to business school. My first career was actually not in tech; it was in medical devices. I was a GM for a company based out of France and also overseeing West Africa business for them. After doing that, I moved back to the US, launched my own startup, which didn't work out, and then I moved to the Bay Area roughly eight years ago. In the Bay Area I wanted to become a PM, which was really hard to get into. At first, I joined a startup, series a company, became head of product for them, and then join Slack as the first PM on their growth team. Then from their, help scale the growth team at Slack. When I joined revenue was around 50 million; when I left roughly four years ago was 10x that. And then after Slack I recently joined YouTube Google about two years ago. At Google I'm a product lead at YouTube, where I'm driving a product called Primetime Channels, which actually recently launched in November in the US. And in that product, we're bringing streaming services to YouTube so that users can watch their favorite movies, shows, and sports content.
turns.zh: 好的，我很乐意分享。简单介绍一下背景，我在海地长大，在大学学习计算机科学，后来读了商学院。我的第一份职业并非科技领域，而是医疗设备行业。我曾担任一家法国公司的总经理，负责西非业务。之后，回到美国创办了自己的初创公司，但未获成功。大约八年前，我搬到湾区，立志成为产品经理，但当时这个领域很难进入。起初，我加入一家A轮融资的初创公司，担任产品负责人，随后加入Slack，成为其增长团队的首位产品经理。之后，我帮助Slack的增长团队扩展规模。加入Slack时，营收约5000万美元；四年前离职时，营收已增长十倍。离开Slack后，两年前我加入了YouTube Google团队，担任YouTube的产品负责人，负责推动“黄金时段频道”产品，该产品于11月在美国正式上线。我们正将流媒体服务引入YouTube，用户可以观看喜爱的电影、剧集和体育内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. The reason that I think we pushed this schedule of this podcast recording out is because you've been working on that product for many months and I'm glad to hear that it's finally launched. How did the launch go?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们之所以推迟播客录制日期，是因为你为这个产品努力了数月，如今终于上线了，真是令人欣喜。上线情况如何？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: So far so good. It's really exciting to take a product from nothing to something.
turns.zh: 目前进展顺利。将一个产品从无到有地打造出来，实在令人兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Especially at a company like Google.
turns.zh: 尤其是在谷歌这样的公司。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah. And then over time we are adding more exciting content onto the product. We just recently you announced that we're adding NFL Sunday Ticket in 2023 to primetime channels and also to YouTube TV. It's been a really exciting project.
turns.zh: 是的。随着时间推移，我们会为产品添加更多精彩内容。最近宣布，2023年NFL周日票将上线黄金时段频道和YouTube TV，这真是个令人兴奋的项目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's awesome. I bet there's a lot of stories there, but I know you can't talk too much about what's happening at Google, so we'll move on. I like the point that you made about joining a startup, like you were trying to get into product management and you joined a startup as their first PM. I think you mentioned that's how you got into the PM path or I guess... Correct me if I'm wrong, but that's an interesting example of one of the paths into product management: joining a startup, getting into product there.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我敢说你有很多精彩故事，但我知道你不能过多谈论谷歌的动态，所以我们继续。之前你提到加入初创公司，试图进入产品管理领域，最终成为首位PM。这是不是进入PM路径的一个典型案例？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Not as their first PM, but I joined as one of their first PMs. Yeah.
turns.zh: 不算是首位PM，但我是首批PM之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As one of their first PMs?
turns.zh: 作为首批PM之一？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's something I hear often is just one of the paths to product management is join a startup, start doing product, and then you're a PM. And then you have a PM title on your resume and you can now join other companies. Is that something you found or anything you can take away from that experience?
turns.zh: 听说加入初创公司、参与产品开发，然后成为产品经理，这是进入产品管理领域的一条常见路径。之后你就能在简历上写上PM头衔，再去其他公司应聘。这是你的亲身经历，还是从他人的经历中总结出来的？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah. It's really, really hard to get into product and there isn't a really set path to do that. What I've seen is the path that we just talked about, join a startup and then from there go into different companies. And then the other path that is typical is being at a company and then switching product management, especially if you develop domain expertise and there's a need for a PM. So, that's even more frequent. Of course there's also acquisitions that sort of thing, but making that initial transition is really hard.
turns.zh: 是的。进入产品领域确实非常困难，也没有一条固定的路径。我见过我们刚刚讨论的那条路径——加入初创公司，然后跳槽到其他公司。另一种常见路径是留在原公司，然后转向产品管理，特别是如果你在某个领域积累了专业知识，并且公司正需要PM人才时。这种情况更为常见。当然，还有收购等机会，但最初的转变确实很难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I didn't realize you were the first growth PM at Slack. That is a big role. How did that work out? How did you become the first growth PM at Slack? Was that the first time you're doing growth? What's the story there?
turns.zh: 我之前没意识到你曾是Slack的首位增长型产品经理。这是一个重要的角色。进展如何？你是如何成为Slack的首位增长型产品经理的？这是你第一次负责增长业务吗？能讲讲这段经历吗？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: I joined Slack early 2016 and the role that was available at the time was growth. I did not know anything about growth, but I was like, "Hey, this is my way in at such a great company." So, that's what I joined to do. And then what I did there was really take a learning mindset and lean on mentors, and we can talk about that to really learn the practice of growth and applied for Slack.
turns.zh: 我2016年初加入Slack，当时空缺的职位是增长团队。我对增长业务一无所知，但当时就想：“嘿，这是在这么棒的公司入职的好机会。”所以我决定接受这个职位。在那里，我保持学习的心态，借助导师的指导，努力掌握增长实践，最终成功应聘。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. We're definitely going to talk about some of those things. Just thinking about that experience and that ride at Slack, what's like maybe the most tangible memory or most, I don't know, interesting story of just riding that rocket ship of Slack growth as one of their early PMs?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们肯定会深入探讨这些经历。回顾在Slack的这段历程，作为早期PM之一，见证Slack增长势头最明显的记忆或最有趣的故事是什么？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: There's many, many stories. My experience was I got in, didn't know much about growth, and then through mentorship, in particular, one mentor, Bangaly Kaba, sort of learned how to apply growth frameworks to my work. And then when I did that within six months, I was able to ship changes in the new user experience, especially on mobile. That moved the needle by a lot, like double-digit percentages within your [inaudible 00:08:38]. And we're talking about top line metrics like activation. It was just interesting being able to have such impact very quickly at a company, and then the company itself went through all these milestones. I mentioned I joined 50 million, the next thing it's a hundred, and it keep doubling, going through a public offering. So, there's just so many stories that are unique to hyper growth.
turns.zh: 有很多故事。我的经历是加入公司时对增长业务知之甚少，但通过导师指导，尤其是Bangaly Kaba的指导，我学会了如何将增长框架应用到工作中。在六个月内，我成功优化了新用户体验，尤其是在移动端。这带来了显著的提升，比如激活率等关键指标在[听不清00:08:38]期间翻了一番。我们谈论的是顶级指标，比如激活率。能在一家快速发展的公司如此迅速地产生影响，这非常有趣，随后公司又经历了多个里程碑。我提到的加入时用户数是5000万，接下来是1亿，不断翻倍，最终上市。超高速增长的经历确实有很多独特的故事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You also didn't mention in your background all these kind of extracurricular activities that you have. I've always been impressed with how much time you put into things that are kind of just volunteer projects on the side. Can you talk about some of the stuff that you do outside of your actual day job?
turns.zh: 你的背景中还提到了许多课外活动。我一直很钦佩你能投入大量时间参与这些兼职志愿项目。能谈谈你工作之外的活动吗？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Outside of my work at YouTube now and also my family and young kids, I'm also involved with two nonprofits that I co-founded. Both of them are actually about improving diversity in tech, which is something I'm really passionate about. The first one is called CodePath and it's improving diversity for software engineers, and the second one is Black PMs focused on product management. With CodePath specifically, what we do is we train over 5,000 students every year at universities, typically the university with strong underrepresented populations, and we help them find internships and jobs at top tech companies. And then with Black PMs, we have a community of over a thousand PMs and aspiring PMs and then we help them find community and also grow their skills. Both of them are nonprofits that I wasn't actually setting out to build them. It's more like I had the need myself or I wish I had those sort of support when I was earlier in my career. And then I started helping folks and then one thing led to the other, especially my co-founders, and then these became big.
turns.zh: 除了我在YouTube的工作，以及我的家庭和年幼的孩子，我还参与了两家由我联合创立的非营利组织。这两个组织实际上都是致力于提升科技行业多样性的，这也是我非常热衷的事情。第一个组织叫CodePath，致力于为软件工程师提升多样性；第二个组织Black PMs专注于产品管理领域。具体来说，CodePath每年为5000多名大学生提供培训，通常选择那些少数族裔群体代表性不足的大学，帮助他们在顶尖科技公司找到实习和工作机会。至于Black PMs，我们拥有超过1000名产品经理和有志于此的人士组成的社区，帮助他们寻找行业资源并提升技能。这两个非营利组织并非我刻意创立的，更多是出于自身需求——我希望在职业生涯早期能获得类似支持。后来我开始帮助他人，一件事接着一件事，尤其是在联合创始人的助力下，这些组织逐渐发展壮大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds like a classic startup story, solve your own problem and turns into a larger and larger thing. I think I try to work with Black PMs as much as I can, and I know that you recently had a conference, which is so cool. I don't know, it was a really big conference that you organized. I don't know how you all had time for all that, but anything you can share about this conference and is there another one coming?
turns.zh: 这听起来像个典型的创业故事，先解决自己的问题，再逐渐做大。我觉得我尽可能多地与Black PMs合作，我知道你们最近举办了一场会议，太棒了。我不知道，那是一场规模宏大的会议，由你们组织的。真不知道你们怎么有时间做这么多事，但能分享一下这次会议的情况吗？还有下一场会议的计划吗？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Now we have a really good team at Black PMs. The CEO, Brittany Bankston and the team, Benin Saffo and others, have helped put together that amazing conference that I was able to attend. It's amazing that it's hard for underrepresented community to see themselves in podcasts, at conferences, at speakers, that sort of thing. So, it gave that opportunity and it also enables us to realize that you're not alone. Because part of why I created Black PMs with my co-founders is... Actually, I'll tell you the story. (00:11:17): I think it was around 2016, I was at a barbecue. I met another Black PM, Maryanna Quigless. I didn't know her and I was like, "Oh, you're a Black PM at Facebook. How many of you are there at the company?" And we're joking and we're like, "Hey, I bet we can list all the Black PMs we know." And we had basically roughly 15 between the two of us and we're like, "Hey, let's bring them all together in a room and to have a community." From there, started helping each other and that grew from 15 to now over a thousand.
turns.zh: Black PMs现在有一个非常出色的团队。首席执行官布列塔尼·班克斯顿和团队成员贝宁·萨福等人，成功举办了那场精彩的会议，我有幸参加了。令人惊讶的是，少数族裔群体在播客、会议、演讲者等场合中难得看到自己的身影。因此，这次会议为他们提供了机会，也让我们意识到自己并不孤单。因为我和联合创始人创建Black PMs的初衷是……实际上，我来讲讲这个故事。（00:11:17）：我想是在2016年左右，我参加了一场烧烤聚会。遇到了另一位Facebook的黑人产品经理玛丽安娜·奎格利斯。我之前不认识她，就问：“哦，你是Facebook的黑人产品经理？公司里有多少位？”我们开玩笑说：“嘿，我打赌我们能列出认识的所有黑人产品经理。”结果我们俩加起来大概有15位，然后就想：“嘿，把他们都召集到一个房间里，组建一个社区吧。”从那时起，我们开始互相帮助，成员从15人发展到如今的1000多人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Amazing. It's really inspiring, the work that you do. I don't know how you find time for all this. I love that you found ways to kind of delegate this and have other people run the program now.
turns.zh: 哇。太了不起了。你做的工作真的很鼓舞人心。我不知道你怎么有时间做这些事。我很欣赏你能找到办法授权他人，让其他人来运营这些项目。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah. Now, I'm mostly on the board of these organizations. We have really solid teams for both Black PMs and CodePath, and the teams are just really amazing.
turns.zh: 是的。现在，我主要担任这两个组织的董事会成员。Black PMs和CodePath都有非常出色的团队，团队成员都非常棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This touches on the stuff that I want to spend most of our time on our chat, which is around mentorship and just generally becoming a stronger product manager through all the ways you can become a stronger product manager. You mentioned you had a lot of great mentors. I've heard from other people, you've been a great mentor to them and you've also just been really successful at a number of really world-class companies. What I want to chat about is just, what have you found to be the most important skills to develop as a PM as you advance in your career, and then how to actually build those skills partly with mentorship, partly other ways? Maybe just to start, what have you found to be the most important skills in your career that have most helped you advance in your career and other PMs around you?
turns.zh: 这涉及到我希望我们在聊天中重点探讨的内容——导师指导，以及如何通过各种方式提升产品经理能力。你提到自己曾有过许多优秀的导师。我也听其他人说，你自己也是一位出色的导师，并且在多家世界级公司取得了巨大成功。我想聊聊的是，随着职业生涯发展，成为更优秀的产品经理最重要的能力是什么？又该如何通过导师指导和其他途径来培养这些能力？或许可以先从这个问题入手：在你的职业生涯中，哪些最重要的技能帮助你获得了晋升，也为身边的产品经理带来了积极影响？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: In terms of skills, I think of it in terms of two buckets. One are IQ skills, intellectual skills, like what sometimes people call hard skills. And then the other things are the EQ skills, oftentimes called soft skills. What I've seen in my career is that early on, I leaned more into the hard skills, the IQ stuff. That was what was most helpful to me. And then later on, I spent more time getting better at the EQ skills. The reality with PMs is that within each of these buckets, there's so many skills and then you can feel overwhelmed, so my advice is really just start skill by skill. What I did specifically is I joined Slack, I was in ICPM. When you join a new company, especially if you're earlier in the mid-career, you really want to get good at things like execution, IQ skills, execution, product sense, strategy. So, those were critical for me, especially my first year at Slack. (00:13:51): The other skill that I'll also call out, which nobody talks about for some reason, is interview skills, because so much of what gives you a chance to become better as a PM is working at a great company. How you get that job beyond networking is actually becoming good at interviewing. If you think about my career, getting into Slack changed my trajectory and I was able to do that because I got slightly somewhat good enough at interviewing. I barely got the job and then I was really good at execution and got better at these other things, product sense, strategy, et cetera. In that phase, the things that I was working on, as I mentioned earlier, were things like improving user activation. So, it relies on those skills: identifying the opportunities, running experiments, executing quickly, and so on. That's the first set of skills.
turns.zh: 在技能方面，我将其分为两类。一类是智商技能，即人们常说的硬技能。另一类是情商技能，通常被称为软技能。在我的职业生涯中，早期我更侧重于智商技能，这对我帮助最大。后来，我投入更多精力提升情商技能。产品经理的现实情况是，每个技能类别下都包含诸多细项，可能会让人应接不暇。因此，我的建议是逐一突破每个技能。我具体的做法是加入Slack，加入ICPM（International Community of Product Managers）。当你加入新公司时，尤其是在职业生涯中期阶段，你迫切需要提升执行力、智商技能、产品洞察力和战略思维。这些对我的职业生涯至关重要，尤其是在Slack的第一年。（00:13:51）：另一个我要强调但出于某种原因鲜被提及的技能是面试技巧，因为能让产品经理获得成长机会的关键在于加入一家优秀的公司。除了人脉关系，真正能让你获得这样的机会的，是具备出色的面试能力。回顾我的职业生涯，加入Slack改变了我的发展轨迹，而我能做到这一点，是因为我在面试技巧上取得了不错的成绩。我勉强拿下了那份工作，随后在执行力等其他方面不断提升，进而掌握了产品洞察力和战略思维等技能。在那个阶段，我专注于提升用户激活率。这依赖于以下技能：识别机遇、开展实验、快速执行等。这些构成了第一组技能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before we move on, and the second set is EQ, right? Is that where you're going?
turns.zh: 在我们继续之前，第二组技能是情商技能，对吧？你接下来要讲这个吗？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. Maybe just one quick thread I want to pull on is this interviewing skill. That's really interesting. Your point here is you're not... And I think you're going to get to this of just how to get better at these skills. You mentioned one of the best ways is to be surrounded by amazing people who can help you get better at these skills, but you won't get there if you can't actually get into a company like Slack. Is there something you've found to be useful in building these interview skills? When you say interview, it's being interviewed, not interviewing other people, like passing these interview tests.
turns.zh: 好的。或许我可以快速提一下面试技巧。这真的很有趣。你的观点是，你不是……我觉得你接下来要讲如何提升这些技能。你提到最好的方法之一是身处优秀的人才圈，他们能帮助你提升技能，但如果你无法进入Slack这样的公司，就无法实现这一目标。在培养这些面试技巧方面，你发现了哪些有效的方法？这里说的面试，是指被面试，而不是面试别人，也不是通过面试测试。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I guess what have you found has been most helpful in helping you become a better interviewee?
turns.zh: 是啊。我想你发现的最有帮助的事情是什么？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: When people tell me, "Hey, I'm going to a interview at this company." First question I ask is, "How many mock interviews have you done?" And the answer typically is zero. It's, "Oh, I read a bunch of stuff. I practiced in my head." But I'm like, "How many actual mock interviews have you done?" And I would recommend people to do dozens of those mock interviews. Now, the other thing about practice is it's always better if you deliberate practice. If you mock interview with somebody who's actually good at interviewing, then you'll get better faster. But even if you don't do that, just going from zero mocks to practicing in your head to actually doing mocks with peers and others is going to get you to another level. And then the other thing I'll say is interviewing can be quite traumatic and difficult for a lot of people, even me. I mean before I got this job, I interviewed at Google, I don't know how many times, over the last decade or two.
turns.zh: 当人们告诉我，“嘿，我要去这家公司面试了。” 我问的第一个问题是，“你做过多少次模拟面试？” 而答案通常是零次。他们会说：“哦，我读了很多资料，在脑子里练习过。” 但我会问，“你真正做过的模拟面试有多少次？” 我建议人们多做几十次模拟面试。现在，关于练习的另一件事是，如果你有针对性地练习会更好。如果你和真正擅长面试的人进行模拟面试，你会进步得更快。但即使你不这样做，从零次模拟到在脑子里练习，再到和同行或其他人一起实际进行模拟面试，也会让你提升到一个新的水平。然后我想说的是，面试对很多人来说可能非常痛苦和困难，甚至对我来说也是如此。在得到这份工作之前，我面试了谷歌多少次，我不记得了，但在过去的十年或二十年里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wait. You're saying you're interviewed at Google many times and you didn't get in then you kept looking for new opportunities?
turns.zh: 等等。你是说你多次面试谷歌，但都没成功，然后你就继续寻找新的机会了？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah. I graduated from MIT and I think even since internship times in '07, I'd interviewed for roles at Google and I didn't get those roles or Meta or various other companies. It's because I wasn't good at interviewing and I didn't know people at those companies. By the way, most things you do, people give you some feedback so you can get better at it, but interviewing you never get any feedback. That's the thing people don't talk about, but it's actually an important skill or a barrier to underrepresented folks.
turns.zh: 是的。我从麻省理工学院毕业后，我认为从2007年的实习时期开始，我就面试过谷歌、Meta和其他许多公司的职位，但都没有成功。这是因为我不擅长面试，而且我不认识那些公司的任何人。顺便说一句，大多数你做的事情，人们会给你一些反馈，这样你就能提高，但面试你永远得不到任何反馈。这是人们不常谈论的，但这实际上是一项重要的技能，也是弱势群体面临的障碍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To actually get feedback?
turns.zh: 得到反馈吗？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah. You won't get feedback after an interview at any company.
turns.zh: 是的。你在任何公司的面试后都不会得到反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really good insight of just people see you join a YouTube and are like, "Oh, yeah, of course he's going to get into YouTube." But you're saying that you actually tried to interview and get into Google many times and it took a number of attempts and advancing your career a little bit before you actually... So, don't feel so discouraged if it doesn't work out.
turns.zh: 这真是一个很好的见解，人们看到你加入YouTube会说，“哦，是啊，他当然能进入YouTube。” 但你是在说你实际上多次尝试面试谷歌，经过多次尝试和在职业生涯中取得一些进步后，你才最终成功了。所以，如果不成功，也不要太灰心。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In terms of this mock, that's a really important point of just actually doing the interviews, like practicing, practicing, practicing. Not just reading questions but actually testing and practicing interview. If you were interviewed at a big company, there's a lot of videos out there of like, "Here's the questions they ask. Here's what they look for." And you're saying find people that work at the company and do these sorts of interviews with them. For companies that are smaller that maybe don't... It's not as obvious what they're going to ask you. Do you have any advice on how to find someone to do a mock interview with or how or what to actually be talking through?
turns.zh: 就模拟面试而言，真正做面试，练习，练习，练习才是最重要的。不要只是阅读问题，而是要实际测试和练习面试。如果你在大公司面试，网上有很多视频，比如“他们问的问题是什么。他们在寻找什么。” 而你是在说找在公司工作的人和他们进行这种面试。对于较小的公司，可能不太清楚他们会问你什么。关于如何找到人进行模拟面试，或者如何或谈论什么内容，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah, it's hard at smaller companies. However, I think interviewing even at bigger companies will help you [inaudible 00:18:04]. A lot of the times the bigger companies have more rigorous processes. So if you can do well there, then it is a bit easier elsewhere. But the key is really that practice part, which people overlook.
turns.zh: 是啊，在小公司确实挺难的。不过我觉得即便是在大公司面试，也能对你有所帮助[00:18:04语音不清]。大公司的面试流程通常更严格。所以如果你能在那里表现出色，那么在其他地方也会相对容易些。但关键在于实践环节，这一点却常被人们忽视。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. Well, maybe one last question there and we'll move on. Do you have any favorite resources or just advice of where to go find the questions to mock interview with and then who do you look forward to do these interviews with, like just find someone at the company or one of these larger companies that you respect to mock interview with?
turns.zh: 好的。那最后再问一个问题，然后我们就结束。你们有没有喜欢的资源或者建议去哪里找模拟面试的题目？比如找公司内部的人，或者是一些大公司的人来模拟面试？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: I mentor a bunch of people who talk about various communities that exist out there. I can follow up on those, but there are large communities of people prepping for these companies. The key is really just being a part of a community and doing the mocks. And then the last thing I'll say on this is interviewing is hard and especially, I think, hard for underrepresented folks because it's high pressure. It's high stress, high ambiguity-
turns.zh: 我指导过很多人，他们提到了很多现有的社区。我可以跟进这些信息，但现在有很多为这些公司做准备的人组成的大型社区。关键就是要融入这样的社区，进行模拟面试。最后我想说的是，面试确实很难，尤其是对少数族裔群体来说更是如此，因为压力太大了。高压环境、高强度挑战、模糊的标准——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So much stress.
turns.zh: 压力太大了。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: ... coming into a company. I've gone into companies like an interview and then the whole panel, nobody looks like me. I walk into the cafeteria, nobody looks like me. And then you are interviewing and you have all this self-talk about, "Hey, do I even want to work there? Will I belong," while you're trying to solve complex problems. So, that's also the other part companies don't think about. What I do, like folks at Black PMs that I coach, is really help them find groups of people, like small groups. Let's say three of us, et cetera, three to five, and then you practice with that group who are going through the process. And because you like the people, then it makes it a bit more fun and it also can help you prep for your own nerves in those interviews.
turns.zh: ……进入一家公司。就拿我自己来说，我去面试，然后整个面试小组里没人长得像我。走进食堂，也没人像我。然后你在面试过程中，脑子里会不断自我怀疑：“嘿，我真的想在这里工作吗？我能融入吗？”而与此同时，你还要解决复杂的问题。这也是很多公司忽视的另一个方面。我所做的，比如我指导的Black PMs团队，就是帮助他们找到志同道合的小团体。假设有三个人左右，五个人左右，然后和这个团队一起练习。因为你喜欢这些人，所以过程会更有趣，也能帮助你克服面试时的紧张情绪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I'm hearing is, and I know we hear this all the time, if you're, say, a Black product manager, it's so much harder to not just get in because there's potentially bias at the company, but you're just psychologically not feeling as comfortable because nobody looks like you. You're worried that they're going to have bias against you. Is that what you find?
turns.zh: 我听到的是——我知道我们经常听到这种说法——如果你是一名黑人产品经理，要想进入大公司确实更难，不仅因为可能存在偏见，还因为心理上你会觉得不自在，因为周围没人长得像你。你会担心他们会对你有偏见。你觉得这是不是你的经历？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah, that has been my experience and it's also what I hear from a lot of people I mentor.
turns.zh: 是的，这就是我的经历，也是我指导的许多人的共同感受。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Your advice there, and this is helpful to anyone also, is just practice even more because that's probably the best way to get over that as much as you can.
turns.zh: 你的建议对任何人都有帮助，那就是多多练习，因为这是尽可能克服这些心理障碍的最佳方法。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah. You want to basically practice so much that even at your worst, you're good enough. I've always felt like most interviews, I literally did my worst. It's just that it was good enough to pass. You're so stressed out, you don't relate to the person, et cetera.
turns.zh: 是的。基本上你要练习到即使在你状态最差的时候，也足够优秀。我自己的大多数面试都是发挥失常，但好在还是能通过。压力太大了，你和面试官没有共鸣，等等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay. Let's go back to the question I asked that I pushed us away from. We were talking about what skills as a PM you want to be focusing on that mostly will help you in your career, and we started with IQ. I wrote a couple notes, so there's the concrete skills, execution, products and strategy, interviewing, and then there's a second bucket of EQ.
turns.zh: 明白了。好的。回到我之前提出但我们跳过的问题。我们之前讨论了作为产品经理，你需要专注的技能，这些技能大多对你的职业生涯有帮助，我们从智商开始。我写了几个笔记，所以具体技能包括执行力、产品和战略、面试，然后还有情商这一块。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: So, the IQ I already talked about. Those are the skills that help me at, especially in my first year at Slack, drive big good experiments, design good product experiences, and then drive results. But then what happened is as I get promoted, managed people and then start having larger scope, then there's a lot of ambiguity and stress that comes in with that increase in scope. And that's where the EQ stuff shows up a lot, specifically things like communications, because it's no longer my team. It's like cross-functional partners, other teams, executives, so you have to communicate all the time to different people. And then the other thing is things like leadership. Now, I'm driving initiatives that involve multiple teams, basic company level OKRs, and then the other thing too is beyond leadership, which is managing your team as well. How do you be a good manager? How do you deal with the ambiguity, stress? How do you influence various people? (00:21:58): These are the EQ skills. What I've seen is, number one, it's much harder to learn these skills than the IQ stuff. The IQ is very intellectual. Sometimes, you just need a mental model, practice a bit. The EQ, I'm still learning these things. It's just like every... I'm trying to get better. Then the other thing beyond it being hard to learn is that the EQ stuff... What you need to focus on is specific to you, so you learn it. You probably work on something different than what I would work on versus if we're both trying to be better at strategy or execution, there's a lot more overlap. So, there's a lot of self-awareness that you need to have to know even what to work on and then you need to continuously practice it.
turns.zh: 接下来，我要讲讲我之前提到的情商（EQ）。这些技能在我的职业生涯中发挥了关键作用，特别是在我加入Slack的第一年——推动重大创新项目、设计优质产品体验，并最终取得成果。但随着晋升、管理团队以及承担更大职责后，我面临着范围扩大的挑战，随之而来的是巨大的不确定性和压力。此时，情商技能就显得尤为重要，比如沟通能力，因为团队不再局限于我的直属成员，还需要与跨职能伙伴、其他团队及高管进行持续沟通。另外，在领导力方面，我需要推动涉及多个团队的项目，制定公司层面的OKR（目标与关键结果），以及管理团队的绩效。如何成为一名优秀的管理者？如何应对不确定性和压力？如何影响不同的人？（00:21:58）——这些都是情商技能的体现。我的经验是，相较于智商（IQ），情商技能的学习难度要高得多。智商更多是知识层面的，有时只需要掌握思维模型并加以练习即可。而情商技能……每个人的侧重点都不同，需要根据自身实际情况进行提升。比如，如果我们都想提升战略或执行能力，那么两者的重叠部分会更多。因此，自我认知至关重要——你需要明确自己的改进方向，并持续磨练这些技能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What did you find was the most important EQ skill for your career that helped you in this journey?
turns.zh: 在你的职业生涯中，哪项情商技能对你帮助最大？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: I don't know if there is one that single-handedly was the most important. I had to develop on many of these things. I can tell you, for example, communication is something that is helpful, especially as I become more senior. What happened for me is, early in my career, it was more about clarity and then conciseness. Then later it became more about how do you tell a story, and then also how do you communicate in an empathetic way. Specifically, you're telling the same story or presentation but to different audiences, and each time you have to adjust it because the CEO will care about this part, the CFO will care about this other part, and so on. I think that's one area where I spend a lot of time. And then the other thing also that has been helpful is the self-awareness part that I mentioned, where through mentorship, especially mentors who were very honest and help me see my blind spots, I was able to see my own patterns. (00:23:54): When I'm under stress, for example, I tend to withdraw and not see anything. So, then you might think I'm disengaged. By the way, in an interview context you might be like, "Oh, does this person even want to work here?" Then once you know these patterns you know, "Okay, I'm stressed right now, but I need to say something so that people see that I'm actually interested in this problem; I'm just thinking through it. Well, let me verbalize my thought process." So, that's me as an example. For you, it might be the opposite. The self-awareness piece has been really helpful and it's something I continue to work on.
turns.zh: 我不确定是否有某项技能能单独称得上最重要。我需要在多个方面进行提升。举个例子，沟通能力对我帮助很大——尤其是随着职位晋升后。早期，我更关注清晰性和简洁性；后来则转向如何讲故事，以及如何以共情的方式沟通。比如，面对不同受众时，你需要调整同样的演示内容，每次都要因材施教——CEO关心某个点，CFO关注另一点。我认为这方面我投入了大量精力。另外，自我认知也很有帮助。通过导师指导，尤其是那些坦诚且能指出我盲点的导师，我逐渐认识到自己的行为模式。（00:23:54）例如，面对压力时，我往往会退缩并忽视问题。这时别人可能会认为我缺乏参与度。在面试中，这可能会让对方质疑“这人是否真心想在这里工作”。但一旦你意识到这些模式，就能调整心态：“好的，我现在压力大，但我需要表达出来，让别人知道我对这个问题很上心，只是需要时间思考。让我把思路说出来。”这就是我的例子。对你们而言，可能相反的模式更适用。但自我认知确实非常重要，也是我持续提升的方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an interesting point that it's important to understand how you react and to figure out what's unique about you that you want to be working on, especially within EQ. For this example you gave about how stress impacts you, how did you actually discover that? Was that this mentor just pointing out, "Hey, Jules, I've noticed this happens," or is there anything else there that maybe folks would find useful?
turns.zh: 这一点很有意思，了解自己的反应方式很重要，尤其是要明确自己在情商方面希望提升的独特之处。对于你提到的压力对你的影响这一例子，你是如何发现的？是这位导师直接指出：“朱尔斯，我注意到你有这种情况”，还是有其他方面值得大家借鉴？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Generally, you need someone to put a mirror in front of you irritably. Sometimes, it's like you hire a coach, I talk to, and they see patterns. I've done group coaching too. In this case specifically, he was a mentor. His name is Lawrence Ripsher. He was head of product at Pinterest and became a mentor and now a close friend. One day I was preparing for... I think I need to do a representation and he was like, "Hey, I've noticed that when you are thinking, you're just quiet. Let me tell you what's going on in my own head when I see that." And then he was like, "Hey, I'm telling myself that he's not interested in what we're doing." And I'm like, "Really? That's the least thing." And then I realized that's a pattern I have. Over time, through him and others, I've also observed other patterns.
turns.zh: 通常，你需要有人不耐烦地在你面前照照镜子。有时候，比如你请了一位教练，跟他们交流，他们会发现一些规律。我也参加过团体辅导。在这个例子中，他是一位导师，名叫劳伦斯·里普谢尔。他曾是Pinterest的产品负责人，后来成为导师，如今也是我的挚友。有一天我在为……做准备时，我想我需要做一个演示，而他说道："嘿，我注意到你思考时总是很安静。让我告诉你，我看到你这样时心里会怎么想。"然后他又说："嘿，我会告诉自己他对我们正在做的事不感兴趣。"我回应道："真的吗？这根本不算什么。"然后我意识到这就是我的一个习惯模式。随着时间推移，通过他和其他人的帮助，我还发现了其他模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I missed this, but was he a manager or just a mentor you had within the company?
turns.zh: 我之前没注意到，但他是公司的经理还是只是一位导师？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: We didn't work at the same company. When I was at Slack, he was head of product at Pinterest. We met at a dinner and then from there, over time, he became a mentor and then we started meeting. When I would hit difficult situations, sometimes I would call him and ask for advice, and then through those interactions he's helped me identify some of my blind spots.
turns.zh: 我们不在同一家公司工作。我在Slack时，他是Pinterest的产品负责人。我们在一次晚餐上认识，后来逐渐成为导师，开始定期见面。当我遇到困难时，偶尔会给他打电话征求建议，通过这些交流，他帮助我识别了自己的一些盲点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, awesome. We're definitely going to talk about mentorship and how to work with a mentor, but let's kind of wrap up this EQ piece. You mentioned within EQ, skills to think about working on communication, leadership, and management. Is there anything else and then is there an example of one of these skills and how, I don't know, it helped you in your career or held you back until you figure out how to work on this?
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。我们肯定会深入探讨导师指导以及如何与导师合作，但先来总结一下情商部分。你提到在情商方面，需要关注沟通、领导力和管理能力等技能。还有其他方面吗？能否举例说明其中一项技能，以及它如何助力你的职业发展，或者反之，如何阻碍你进步？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: High level, I think those buckets are pretty broad: comms, leadership, management. Within each of them, there are various skills like setting vision, strategy, listening to learn, those sort of things. It's actually the type of things that Matt Mochary talked about when he came to speak at your podcast. I mentioned communications was one thing, right? What happened was, when I was at Slack, I was pretty good at writing, which by the way I was terrible at long time ago. It took me years, maybe decade, to get better at. But then when it was time to present... I was fine at presenting, but then if you ask me questions, things would crumble. That even happened to me once at an interview, where I did well presenting and then they asked me a question and then I just gave an answer that wasn't good. (00:27:22): Then the self-awareness part helped me figure out what was going on. For me specifically, I realized whenever people ask me questions, if I didn't know the answer, I would have all this negative self-talk and I basically... You'd ask me a question and of course it could be something like, "Why are we doing it this way?" And it might come from a place of curiosity, you're just like, "Hey, I don't know. Can you tell me why you have more context," right? But in my head I would hear, "I don't agree with this." And that would be my self-talk. "Oh, this person doesn't agree with this," instead of being present and trying to understand where are they coming from and maybe asking follow-ups like, "Hey, thanks for asking the question. Is your concern more about, I don't know, scalability of this approach or is it more that you don't think it's effective even if it's not scalable?" (00:28:10): You know what I mean? For someone else, it might be the easiest thing, but for me it took me months and months to, first of all, figure out that I had this pattern. And then once I figured out the pattern, it took also a while to now actually act on it so that now I'm comfortable. If you ask me a question, sometimes I don't know and I'll say, "Hey, let me get back to you." Sometimes I don't know and I'll say, "Hey, I don't know, but here's what I'm thinking." This little thing that may seem so obvious to you took me a while and different people have different versions of these blockers.
turns.zh: 高层面上，我觉得这些能力领域相当宽泛：沟通、领导力、管理。在每个领域内，又包含诸如设定愿景、制定战略、倾听以学习等各种技能。这其实正是马特·莫查里（Matt Mochary）在贵播客演讲时所谈及的内容。我提到过沟通能力，对吧？当时的情况是，我在Slack公司时写作能力不错——说实话，我很久以前写作水平很糟糕。花了好多年甚至十年才有所提升。但到了要做演示的时候……我演示没问题，但要是有人提问，情况就糟糕了。这种情况甚至在面试中出现过——我演示表现不错，但一被问问题就答得不理想。（00:27:22）那时自我意识帮我意识到问题所在。具体来说，我发现每当有人提问时，我如果不知道答案，就会陷入消极的自我对话。比如有人问“为什么我们要这样做？”，这可能出于好奇，但你可能会说“不知道，你能不能讲讲背景？”但我在脑子里却会想“我不同意这种做法。”而不是专注当下，试图理解对方的出发点，并追问“你为什么这么担心？是担心可扩展性，还是觉得即使不可扩展也不管用？”（00:28:10）懂我的意思吧？对别人来说可能很简单，但我花了好几个月才首先发现自己有这种模式。发现模式后，又花了很久才真正改进，现在我能从容应对了。遇到不知道的问题时，有时我会说“等下回复你”，有时会说“虽然不知道，但我有个想法。”这么简单的事，对你来说可能显而易见，但我却花了很久才领悟。不同人对这些障碍的理解也各不相同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Linear. Let's be honest, the issue tracker that you're using today isn't very helpful. Why is it that always seems to be working against you instead of working for you? Why does it feel like such a chore to use? Well, Linear is different. It's incredibly fast, beautifully designed, and it comes with powerful workflows that streamline your entire product development process, from issue tracking all the way to managing product roadmaps. Linear is designed for the way modern software teams work.
