In short, it just works. Linear is the default tool of choice among startups and it powers a wide range of large established companies such as Versatile, Retool, and Cash App. See for yourself by product teams describe using Linear as magical. Visit linear.app/lenny to try linear for free with your team and get 25% off when you upgrade. That's linear.app/lenny. (00:29:54): I love these stories and this is a good segue to start talking a bit about not just what skills to focus on, but how to actually get better at these things and identify these patterns in yourself. There's like a bunch of skills we just named, so let's also talk about where you think you start as you're starting off as a PM, which skills to focus on first, second, third. Let me just ask this broad question. We've talked about all these different skills PM should have. What have you found to be most effective broadly at building these skills in your career?
turns.zh: 本期节目由Linear赞助。说实话，你现在使用的issue tracker（问题追踪工具）实在不够给力。为什么它总像是在跟你作对，而不是为你服务？为什么用起来总让人觉得无比繁琐？Linear则截然不同。它速度极快，设计精美，还配备了强大的工作流系统，能全面优化你的产品开发流程——从issue追踪到产品路线图管理，全程无缝衔接。Linear专为现代软件团队的工作方式而设计。用户们最爱它的快捷键组合、高效的GitHub集成、能真正推动进展的迭代周期，以及让所有人保持信息同步的内置项目更新。简而言之，它就是高效易用之选。Linear是初创公司的默认选择工具，同时也为Versatile、Retool、Cash App等大型成熟企业提供支持。亲自体验一下吧——产品团队们都称赞它堪称"神器"。访问linear.app/lenny，即可与团队免费试用Linear，升级后还可享25%折扣。就是linear.app/lenny。（00:29:54）：我特别喜欢这些案例分享。这里可以顺势聊聊PM职业发展的关键点——不只是要明确专注的技能方向，更要掌握提升这些技能的有效方法，以及如何在自身实践中识别出这些模式。我们刚刚列举了诸多技能，现在就来探讨初入PM领域的你该如何合理分配优先级。先从最基础的技能讲起，再逐步深入。让我抛出一个开放性问题：PM需要具备的各种技能中，你发现哪些在职业生涯中最有效？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: I will share my approach. It might not work for everyone and later when we talk about strengths and weaknesses. You might see why that works for me. What I do specifically is when I'm trying to learn something new, I try to think about what is an outcome that I could drive. And if I drive this outcome, it will be proof that I'm better at this thing. If we go back to this story of when I joined Slack, I didn't know anything, literally anything about growth. And I was telling myself, "I hope they don't fire me." But then the outcome I wanted is, within six months, I wanted to ship enough experiments that were successful, that drove activation by, let's say, X percent. So, that's very concrete. (00:31:06): Then once I have this outcome, I work backwards to figure out how am I going to do that. One of the things we can talk about later when we talk about strength is that, for me, I'm really good at asking questions. What I do then is I start asking questions like, "Okay, I'm trying to drive activation for Slack. What are some frameworks that I should use to drive activation? What are best practices? What are examples?" I have a sense of the kind of question that, if I were to answer them, I'd be able to drive the outcome. And then what I do is I read a little bit, not a lot about the topic, just to make sure I'm asking the right question. Then I refine my questions and then I find the best people in the field and I just go talk to them. That's where we'll talk later about the mentorship part. (00:31:54): In the case of activation, I was like, "Okay, what's the company that defined growth?" At the time, Facebook. "Who are the people that I can reach out to that do growth at Facebook?" And one of them was Bangaly Kaba and also Adriel Frederick who spoke at your podcast. I had met both of them at a random event. Then I'm like, "I need to find a way to have a chat with these folks and to help answer those questions with them." So, that's what I did with Bangaly in particular and also Adriel to a certain extent. I then learned, "Okay, here are frameworks to use for growth." For example, understand, identify, execute. Spend a lot more of your time understanding why people aren't staying on Slack versus anything else, so then I had pointers. (00:32:40): Once I have the pointers, then I try to go through the thing. I'm like, "Okay, now let me..." I call the user researcher, "Hey, can we do a research on people who are signing up on Slack?" Data analysts, let's look at the data. What correlates with activation?" Those sort of things. Then after I go through a look, where I actually see results, whether they're good or bad, I go back to the mentor and I'm like, "Hey, I did this. It was actually successful. Thanks a lot." Now, I'm thinking about this other problem." I keep going and that's how I rinse and repeat, and over time I drive the outcome and I also know I'm getting better at this thing by working with the experts.
turns.zh: 我会分享一下我的方法。它可能并不适用于所有人，在我们讨论优势和劣势时，你或许会明白为什么它对我有效。具体来说，我在学习新事物时，会先思考自己能达成什么样的成果。如果我能实现这个成果，就证明我在这方面更擅长了。再说回我加入Slack时的故事，当时我对增长策略一无所知，满脑子都是“希望他们别开除我”。但我设定的目标是，在加入后的六个月内，通过成功的实验提升用户活跃度，比如达到X%的增长率。这目标非常具体。（00:31:06）然后，确定目标后，我会倒推如何实现它。谈到优势时，要知道我很善于提问。比如，我会问自己：“我要如何提升Slack的用户活跃度？应该用哪些框架？最佳实践是什么？有成功案例吗？”通过这些问题，我能确保自己提的问题能真正推动成果。接着，我会阅读相关资料，快速了解领域知识，再优化问题，最后找到该领域的专家进行深度交流。这部分我们稍后再详细探讨。（00:31:54）以用户活跃度为例，我会思考：“Facebook是增长策略的标杆吗？” 当时Facebook的Bangaly Kaba和Adriel Frederick（曾做客你的播客）是我能联系到的人。我在一次随机活动中结识了他们，于是决定主动联系他们，共同探讨问题。通过与Bangaly的交流，我掌握了增长策略的框架，比如“理解、识别、执行”。比如，深入研究用户为何流失到其他平台，这为我指明了方向。（00:32:40）得出初步结论后，我会组织行动：邀请用户研究员研究Slack的新用户行为，数据分析师分析相关数据，寻找激活用户的关联因素……每次验证成果后，无论成功与否，我都会向导师汇报：“我完成了任务，效果不错，感谢指导。” 然后再转向下一个挑战。如此循环往复，最终达成目标，同时不断提升自己的能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a few interesting takeaways there. One, is that you kind of create a forcing function for yourself to learn a thing. It's like, "Hey, I'm going to learn this thing. Let's create a goal that my ass is on the line to hit and then that's going to force me to go figure this out." And then two, it's interesting how often you come back to mentors and other people around you helping you out, which is a really good reminder. You don't have to figure things out for yourself; there's people out there that know these things and they're happy to help. A question I want to ask and I'll save this, because I we're going to talk about mentorship specifically a little bit later, just like how to find these people. Not everyone has access to Bangaly and Adriel, and I'm curious just how you found these folks, how you recommend other people find folks like that. But that's an awesome example. One tactic you're talking about here is just work backwards from a forcing function you've created for yourself to learn a thing. And in this case, what was it you were trying to learn? You were trying to learn growth, is that right?
turns.zh: 其中有几个有趣的启发点。第一点是，你可以为自己创造一个强制学习的机制。比如说：“嘿，我要学习这个东西。设定一个必须达成的目标，这样就能迫使自己去钻研。”第二点是，人们经常向导师和身边的人求助，这确实是个很好的提醒。没必要凡事都亲力亲为，总有懂行的人愿意伸出援手。接下来我想问个问题（先留着，因为我们稍后会专门探讨导师机制），比如如何找到这些高手？不是每个人都能接触到班加利和阿德里尔这样的导师，我很好奇你是如何找到这些人才的，能否给其他人一些建议。不过他们的例子确实很棒。谈到你提到的策略时，就是从为自己设定的强制学习机制倒推。当时你想学习什么？你当时想在激活新用户的上下文中学习增长策略，后来又想在变现环节中探索如何推动收入增长，而非单纯增加用户数。再后来还想了解如何组建增长团队，如何规划工作流以形成连贯的战略。整个过程就是不断深挖。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah, I was trying to learn growth and I wanted to do it in a context of activation, like new onboarding. And then later I also wanted to learn growth but in a different context, which was monetization. How do you drive revenue growth, not just get more users? And then later it was things like, "How do I learn how to create a growth org? How do I structure my team? How do I set work streams that add up to a coherent strategy?" And you just keep going
turns.zh: 对，我当时想学习增长策略，尤其是在用户激活和新人入职的场景下。后来又想在变现环节中探索如何推动收入增长，而非单纯增加用户数。再后来还想了解如何组建增长团队，如何规划工作流以形成连贯的战略。整个过程就是不断深挖。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In those examples, did you do the same thing, you found people to talk to?
turns.zh: 在这些案例中，你是否也采取了相同的策略，主动寻找导师交流？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. It's the same approach. Sometimes what happens is I have a few mentors that I just keep going to over the years and it's just a top exchange and sometimes I sort of get new mentors who are experts at these new topics. It's a combination of those two things for me. And the thing is you obviously can learn without this approach, but this approach makes you, at least for me, makes me learn so much faster.
turns.zh: 是的。方法是一样的。有时我会持续与多年合作的导师交流，保持深度对话；有时也会结识新领域的专家导师。对我来说，这两种方式相辅相成。当然，不采用这种方法也能学习，但这种方法能显著提升学习效率。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's probably one of the most interesting things I've learned about mentors, and you're touching on this, that people want to help. They're happy to help if people come ask, unless they're just dumb questions or they're just overwhelmed. People are generally very happy to help. People are always worried like, "Why would they spend any time trying to help me with this random thing?" It's really the opposite; they're happy to help.
turns.zh: 这或许是我对导师最深刻的体会之一，而你也提到了这一点——人们乐于助人。只要真诚求教，他们通常都会伸出援手。除非问题太傻或对方负担过重，否则人们普遍乐于助人。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 是的，确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to the EQ and IQ buckets, are there other examples of ways you've learned to improve, say, strategy, execution, product sense, things like that?
turns.zh: 回到情商和智商这两个维度，你是否有其他提升策略的例子，比如战略思维、执行力、产品敏感度等？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Whether you have a mentor or not, there's other things you kind of have to do. For me, for example, one thing I do is I try to identify what's the best practice for something. For example, let's say strategy. There was a phase where I got feedback, "Hey you need to be better at strategy." Then I'm like, "Okay. Well, can you help me understand what are people at this company that was awhile back, where you think have done a great job at strategy or what are examples of artifacts?" Then I get these artifacts and I reverse engineering them. I try to think, "Okay, what are the top questions, the answer? Maybe I'm not answering all these questions. How do they do it?" And you start seeing the patterns like, "This person did it in a memo, this person did it in a deck." So, it's not about the format, but what is it about? Then this person had a lot of data, this person is quantitative, qualitative. So, that's a big part of what I do as well. It's true for all these things. (00:36:47): For execution, it would be things like me attending another PMs meeting. "Oh, I heard this person is amazing at executing. Let me just see how they're on a meeting." And then you're like, "Whoa, things we didn't notice." Or somebody is great at communicating and I'm like, "Okay. Well, did you send this email? It's great. Let me save it." I'd have docs where I saved templates of things, and a lot of the reason, I think, people don't learn through osmosis that way is because one is you're not at a company where you can see great artifacts sometimes. That's why I mentioned if you can get a better company, do that. The other thing, too, is even if you see the greatness around you, some people don't try to break it down, to understand: "Why is this one great and not that one?" So, I actually do spend a lot of time every week reflecting like, "Oh, I saw these docs that were great or I saw this presentation this person gave." I sometimes crash presentation audits PMs give to executives, just to see how they handle questions or these sort of things. A lot of it is just spending time observing as well.
turns.zh: 无论你有没有导师，都有一些事情你必须去做。以我为例，我会尝试找出某件事的最佳实践。例如，战略规划方面。曾经有人反馈说：“你需要在战略规划方面做得更好。” 我会回应：“好的，那你能帮我理解一下公司里以前做得很好的例子吗？”然后我会收集这些案例，进行逆向工程。我会思考：“最常被问到的问题是什么？答案是什么？或许我有些地方没做到位，他们是如何做到的？” 这样一来，我就能发现一些规律，比如有人用备忘录来做战略规划，有人用演示文稿。关键不在于形式，而在于核心逻辑。（00:36:47） 至于执行力方面，比如参加其他产品经理的会议。“哦，听说某人执行力超强。让我看看他们在会议上的表现。” 这时候你会发现很多意想不到的细节。或者有人沟通能力出色，我会说：“好的，你发的这封邮件太棒了。让我保存下来。” 我会把这些模板保存到文档里。之所以很多人无法通过潜移默化学习，是因为有些公司缺乏优秀的范例展示。正因如此，我建议大家如果能加入更优秀的公司，那就去吧。另一方面，即便你身边有优秀的范例，有些人也不会去拆解分析：“为什么这个人做得好而那个做得不好？” 所以我每周都会花大量时间反思，比如：“我看到这些很棒的文档，或者听过某人的演示。” 有时我还会旁听产品经理向高管汇报的演示会，观察他们如何应对提问等情况。这其中很多都是通过观察来学习的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this advice, it's so powerful. Just like, "Who is amazing at this skill? And let me just go watch them and learn from them."
turns.zh: 我太喜欢你的建议了，真是太棒了。就像，“谁在某项技能上特别出色？那我就去观察他们，学习他们的方法。”

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that you touched on here is, and I talk about this a bunch, that one of the benefits of working at a large company like Google, like Slack, is that you have access to a ton of real examples of strategy documents and vision documents and roadmaps and things like that, that once you're out of a company, like me, nobody shares these things publicly because they're sensitive. One of the best benefits of working at a large company is they have access to real life strategy documents, vision documents, things like that, so you should really savor that and collect them and, to your point, just study them. And I love your advice of just working backwards from like, "Okay, here's a strategy that work. What is it about the strategy that I can use when I'm building my strategy? What questions are they answering? How are they structuring it?" Things like that. That's awesome.
turns.zh: 你提到的一个点，我也经常强调，在谷歌、Slack这样的大公司工作的好处之一，就是能接触到大量真实的战略文档、愿景文档、路线图等案例。一旦离开公司，像我这样的人就没法公开分享这些敏感资料了。大公司的另一个好处是，他们能接触到真实的战略文档、愿景文档等，所以你应该好好利用这些资源，收集起来，然后按照你的思路去研究。这太棒了。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Similar to the mentor point, people are actually happy to talk to you. They're even flattered because no one else asked them. "Well, hey, I read your doc. Can we talk about it?"
turns.zh: 和导师机制类似，人们其实很乐意与你交流。他们甚至会感到受宠若惊，因为没人问过他们类似的问题。“嘿，我读了你的文档。我们能聊聊吗？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. Whoever gets the... What PM ever gets someone coming to them? "I love your strategy doc. Tell me all about it. I'd love to talk about that."
turns.zh: 好的。无论谁得到了……首席执行官（PM）让别人来找他谈话的情况有多少呢？“我喜欢你的战略文件。详细跟我讲讲吧。我很想聊聊这个。”

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah. And then the other thing I'll say, too, is a lot of learning happens through the iterations and not by seeing the final product. We all see these products, like the iPhone and name your favorite product, but you don't know what versions they tried and sort of eliminated. And that's the benefit you also get at a company that has great product management. I actually sometimes tell the PM like, "Hey, don't just show me the one you just did. When are you going to do your next strategy? Can I join you then? I just want to sit and watch you write down the outline and just understand your thought process," or "I want to see when you're going to write your next exec update and understand how are you..." And you see them go through these iteration and you see them do things like get feedback that you didn't know they were getting all this feedback from. So, seeing the backstage is also really helpful.
turns.zh: 是啊。我还要说的是，很多学习机会都是在迭代过程中产生的，而不是通过看到最终产品来获得的。我们都见过像iPhone这样的产品，或者你能随口说出喜欢的其他产品，但你并不知道他们尝试过哪些版本，又淘汰了哪些。这就是在拥有出色产品管理的公司能获得的好处。有时我会对PM说：“嘿，别只给我看你刚做好的那个。你们下次的战略规划什么时候开始？我能加入吗？我只想坐下来看着你勾勒大纲，理解你的思路过程。”或者“我想看看你下次写高管汇报时的情况，了解你是如何……” 这样你就能看到他们的迭代过程，还能看到他们获取反馈的场景，而这些反馈你之前可能并不知情。因此，了解幕后情况真的很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting. Just as you're talking, I'm reflecting on how many benefits there are to working at a world class company. You are surrounded by really smart people who you can talk to and ask for advice and watch how they operate. You have access to really incredible documents and artifacts that you can learn from. Also, just the logo on your resume is really powerful for future job opportunities, which then comes back to the interview skills that you talked about and how important it is to be good at that to get into a company like that.
turns.zh: 真有意思。你说话的同时，我就在反思在世界级公司工作的好处。你周围都是非常聪明的人，你可以和他们交流，寻求建议，观察他们的工作方式。你还能接触到极其宝贵的文件和成果，从中学习。此外，你简历上的公司Logo对未来求职也非常有帮助，这又回到了你之前提到的面试技巧，以及掌握这些技巧对进入这样的公司有多么重要。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah, totally.
turns.zh: 是啊，一点不假。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. Okay. What about on EQ? Any examples of how you learned some of those skills that you talked about communication or leadership or management or anything along those lines?
turns.zh: 有意思。好的。那在情商方面呢？你能举些例子，说明你是如何学习你提到的沟通、领导、管理等技能的吗？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah. On the communications side, I read some stuff like Minto's Pyramid Principles. Extremely helpful and I know you had an article on that.
turns.zh: 是啊。在沟通方面，我读了明托的《金字塔原理》。非常有帮助，我知道你写过一篇相关的文章。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: I mentioned also that whenever I see a great email exec update or whatever, I literally save it in a special folder.
turns.zh: 我还提到，每当我看到很棒的邮件高管汇报或其他内容时，我都会把它们保存到一个专门的文件夹里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个做法了。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Also, by the way, I always ask for feedback more than I think many people and I try to see patterns in feedback. For me, one thing I've observed is I tend to write long sentences, coming from a Haitian-French background, but then I see that because I've seen enough feedback that are about it so I see the patterns. Or as I mentioned earlier, I used to not be clear like, "Are you saying this solution or that solution?" It's better sometimes to be wrong but clear than the other way around. That's on the comms side. And then the other things, it's mostly, for me, through mentorship, people like Lawrence helping me be real with myself. I've had a coach for a while and I also do group coaching, which I really love. Right now I'm doing group coaching with a company called Pathways to Leadership. (00:41:48): These sort of things have helped me infer what my strengths and weaknesses are and then work on them. And then one thing I'll say also about the EQ: it was the most frustrating learning for me. For the IQ stuff, within six months, sometimes three months, I can see clear progress when you see enough documents. You see five, six of them, you start seeing 80% of the patterns. But then with the EQ stuff, it's things I've been working on for years. I am better at them, but I still feel like I'm continuing to work on those things. And a lot of it is like lifting weights or building muscles; you have to do it every day or every week. And then if you stop doing it, over time you atrophy again. That's something that people need to acknowledge, too. Give yourself time and then also learn these skills one at a time ideally.
turns.zh:
顺便说一句，我总是比大多数人更频繁地征求反馈意见，并努力从中发现规律。就我个人而言，我发现自己倾向于写长句——这源于我海地法语背景的影响。但通过大量反馈，我逐渐意识到这种倾向，并能从中总结出规律。正如我之前提到的，我曾在沟通方面存在不足，比如会问用户“你说的是这个解决方案还是那个解决方案？”有时候宁愿暂时出错也要确保表达清晰，这比模棱两可要好得多。这只是沟通层面的问题。其他方面主要得益于导师指导，比如劳伦斯帮助我正视自身不足。过去我曾请过教练，也参加过团体辅导课程，非常受益。目前我在一家名为"Pathways to Leadership"的公司参与团体辅导项目。

（00:41:48）这些经历帮助我发现自己的优势与不足，并针对性地进行改进。说到情商培养，这对我来说是最令人沮丧的学习过程。智商相关技能方面，通常通过六个月甚至三个月的系统学习就能看到明显进步——分析五六份文档后，80%的规律就能浮出水面。但情商提升则需要长期努力，就像健身增肌一样，需要每周坚持练习。若松懈下来，就会退步。这是大家必须承认的现实。给自己充足时间，一次专注提升一项技能效果最佳。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, interesting. Can you talk a bit more about that learning skills one at a time? Is your approach just like, "Here's the thing, I'm working on this the next six months. I'm going to focus on that."
turns.zh: 哦，真有意思。你能再详细谈谈一次专注提升一项技能的学习方法吗？你的方法是直接设定目标期限吗？比如，“接下来六个月，我要专注提升这个技能。”

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah. My approach is typically I'll say, "I'm giving myself, I don't know, three months, six months." It depends on what [inaudible 00:43:00] I want to see in my behavior for these things and then I just go all in on that skill. Let's say I wanted to learn strategy, I'll be like, "Okay, I'm giving myself, let's say, six months." Every week, I'm going to do something related to learning strategy. It's going to be maybe I read the strategy for another feature product at my company and you just divide, right? Let's just say there's 10 features or 20, it doesn't matter. You just do one a week, so 20 weeks. You see what I'm saying? And then the other thing is, every week I'm also going to practice it towards my outcome. I'm going to spend, I don't know, three hours a week, maybe one hour a day, just thinking through my own product strategy. And I do that for six months. You do it enough that you get over the hump and then actually develop the skill. Now, the other approach you could take is... What most people do is they read an article on your newsletter or some other place and then like, "Oh, great. I learned an insight." And then you go back to usual.
turns.zh: 是的。我的方法通常是设定期限，比如“给自己三个月、六个月的时间。”这取决于我希望在行为上看到的具体变化。然后全身心投入某项技能。比如我想提升战略思维能力，就设定六个月期限。每周都会围绕战略主题学习，比如阅读公司新产品线的战略规划，拆解分析。总共20周，每周学习一个新点，这样就能突破瓶颈，真正掌握技能。另一种方法是……大多数人会读到新闻通讯或其他文章，感叹“太棒了，我学到了一个深刻见解。”然后又回归日常。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's not like at the end of these six months, you're done. I'm strategy expert, I am good on strategy. To your point, it's building this muscle that will never be fully built. It just will get stronger. And every time you invest time learning something, it gets stronger.
turns.zh: 六个月结束后并不意味着学习结束。我现在是战略专家，但永远无法完全掌握这项技能，只能不断精进。每次投入学习，技能都会有所提升。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. It's not that within six months you are clearly better. Now, you can invest another six months to get to the next level. Or you could say, "Now I'm going to switch focus to another skill and get that one to a similar level."
turns.zh: 是的，没错。并不是说你能在六个月内就明显提升。现在，你可以再投入六个月的时间，达到下一个阶段。或者你可以说：“现在我要把重点转移到另一项技能上，把它提升到类似的水平。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a skill you're working on right now?
turns.zh: 你现在正在钻研哪项技能？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Always working on something. One I can call out is listening. One thing about the EQ stuff, too, by the way is you hear these words, and depending on how familiar you are, you understand or don't understand what it actually means. When I say listening, I'm good at seeking information to solve a problem. If you come to me and you're like, "Hey, Jules, I have this problem," I will know what to listen for and what to ask you. "Hey, Lenny, can you tell me A, B?" And then I'll help you solve the problem. However, there's also different listening patterns, one of which is you just create space for someone. It's not like you're seeking a particular information, just give them space to tell you what they want to tell you. And then the other side of it, too, is you help that person feel heard, "Hey, I feel like you actually understand me and you've heard what I'm saying." So, that's the part I am working on.
turns.zh: 一直在钻研各种技能。顺便说一句，关于情商相关的知识，有些术语你听过，但可能不完全理解其含义。比如“倾听”这个技能，我擅长通过提问获取信息来解决问题。比如你来找我说：“朱尔斯，我遇到了这个问题。”我会知道该倾听什么信息，该问你哪些问题。“嘿，莱尼，你能告诉我A和B吗？”然后我就能帮你解决问题。不过，倾听也有不同的模式。比如，你可以为对方创造空间，让他们畅所欲言，而不必刻意获取特定信息。还有一层含义是，让对方感受到被理解：“嘿，我感觉你真的懂我，听到了我想说的话。” 这正是我目前在努力提升的部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned the Matt Mochary episode. I imagine you've been listening to that, because that has a lot of great advice.
turns.zh: 你提到过马特·莫查里那期节目。我想你一直在听，因为里面有很多很棒的建议。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. It's those kinds of things, right? And then he talked about saying back to people what you heard, asking for more information, et cetera.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。就是这些要点，对吧？他还提到要向对方反馈你听到的内容，要求对方提供更多信息等等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. You mentioned that you asked for feedback from your peers, and I wrote that down. I wanted to double-click on that a little bit. How do you actually approach asking for feedback? Do you sound like a survey? Do you just ask people in meeting? How do you do that?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你提到向同事征求反馈，我把这点记下了。我想再深入探讨一下。你具体怎么去做征求反馈呢？是像做调查问卷那样吗？还是在会议上直接询问？具体怎么操作？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: The feedback piece, it's something that I had to get better at. Over time, I'm asking for it, because what I realize is if people don't feel comfortable with you, they won't give you feedback. It's depending on the risk, right? Especially if it's constructive feedback. By the way, that's also something that's hard about being underrepresented. People sometimes don't have the same natural level of connection with you. I basically learned to go out of my way to make people comfortable giving me feedback. There's different techniques and Matt Mochary also talks about some of them. Sometime it's basically ask in a very specific way, "Hey, I did this presentation. I'm working on, I don't know, having more executive presence. Did you feel that? To which extent did you feel that I showed executive presence?" So, it's a very specific thing versus, "Hey, how did it go?" That's one thing you can do. (00:46:45): Other thing you can do sometimes is you give yourself critical feedback in front of them and then you give them a chance to agree or disagree. "Hey, I feel like this presentation didn't go well for this reason. What do you think? But actually I thought it would've been fine; however, this other thing could have been better." And then the other thing I'll say that is very, very important if you're asking people for feedback is if you manage to get them to take the risk to give you the feedback, your answer has to be enthusiastically grateful. That's the key. What people knew at Slack, Google, et cetera, is if you give me feedback, I'll be like, "Hey, thank you so much. This is super helpful," because people are like, "Oh, he actually likes the feedback." Now, inside, my heart might be melting. I'm like, "Oh, I thought I got better at this." You know what I mean?
turns.zh:
反馈这件事，我确实需要不断提升自己。在长期实践中，我逐渐意识到，如果人们对你感到不自在，他们就不会给你反馈。这取决于风险对吧？尤其是建设性的反馈。说到这，也是作为少数族裔群体面临的挑战之一——人们有时与你的天然联系度不够。我最终学会了主动让别人感到自在，从而获得反馈。马特·莫查里（Matt Mochary）也提到了很多技巧。比如，有时可以用非常具体的方式提问：“嘿，我刚做了这个演示。我正在努力提升自己的高管风范。你有没有感受到这一点？你觉得我展现出高管风范的程度如何？”这样比起简单地问“演示效果如何”要有效得多。

（00:46:45）还有一种方法：先在他们面前给自己一些批评性的反馈，然后让他们有机会提出异议。“我觉得这次演示效果不佳，原因是……你怎么看？不过其实我原本觉得还不错，但这部分可以改进。”

最重要的是，如果你请求别人反馈，成功让他们勇于表达后，你的回应必须充满感激。这是关键。Slack、谷歌等公司的经验表明，如果你真诚地说：“太感谢了，这对我非常有帮助！”，人们会觉得你真心接受反馈。而我内心可能激动不已：“哦，我以为自己已经改进了。” 你懂我的意思吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: But externally, I'm like, "Hey, thank you," and I mean it. I think that's the key that most people don't sort of focus on. And if you get more feedback, then you'll just get better at the things.
turns.zh: 但表面上，我会真诚地说：“谢谢。”我觉得这是大多数人忽视的关键。如果你能获得更多反馈，你就能不断提升自己。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such a good advice, all these very tactical ways of getting actual real feedback from people.
turns.zh: 这些获取真实反馈的实用技巧真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah. And then one thing I'll say, too, by the way, it's harder to get feedback on the EQ stuff, and that's also why it's harder to develop and why a lot of people reach terminal levels in product, because people are like, "Oh, they lack emotional intelligence." They say that in calibration rooms but not in your face, so that's also what you want when you hear feedback. You don't want just to like, "Hey, here's my piece of feedback that I can prove." You also want the part that is like, "Here's how you make me feel or how you come across that... If this is taken out of context, it won't be good for... I don't want this to be shared publicly or taken out of context, but I want you to know." And it could be things like, "Hey, when I talk to you, sometimes I feel like, I don't know, you're angry." And then I'm like, "Oh, really? In what scenario?" And then it's like, "Oh, I was so focused and listening to you intently that I could see now why I come across that way." (00:48:55): But you could literally go your whole career and then nobody ever says these things, right? And that's the kind of feedback that I personally find most helpful is the subjective feedback, because nobody will tell me those things. Once somebody I trust tell me and I'm like... Oh, here's an example. I mentioned earlier I'm good at asking questions. I had somebody ask like, "Tell me. Hey, sometimes when you ask questions, you sound more junior." And I was like, "Huh." And then I can see that because I asked the question plainly like, "Hey, why did you do this or how did you that," instead of also saying where I'm coming from, "Hey, I noticed this blah, blah, why, blah?" You know what I'm saying? Instead of showing I have an understanding of the thing and then asking a follow-up question, I just ask the question bluntly without context and people feel like, "Hey, I'm asking a very basic question." So, that's the kind of feedback that I particularly value.
turns.zh: 是的。顺便说一句，关于情商反馈这件事，我想说的是，要获得这类反馈确实很难。这也是为什么很多人在产品开发中会遇到瓶颈，因为人们会说：“哦，他们缺乏情商。”他们会在评估会议上这么说，但不会当面指责你。这正是你需要的反馈类型。你不希望对方只是说：“嘿，这是我能证明的反馈。”你还需要对方说：“你让我感觉如何，或者你的表现是怎样的……如果脱离上下文，这对……不太好……我不想公开分享这些内容，但我希望你能理解。” 比如，“嘿，有时候和你交谈时，我感觉你好像……生气了。” 然后我会问：“哦，真的吗？在什么情况下？” 对方可能会说：“哦，我当时太专注、太投入地听你说话了，所以现在我才意识到为什么会给人这种印象。” （00:48:55）但你可能一辈子都得不到这样的反馈，对吧？而我个人认为最有价值的反馈就是主观反馈，因为没人会直接告诉我这些。当我信任的人告诉我这些时，我才意识到问题的关键。比如，我之前提到我擅长提问。有人曾说：“告诉我吧。嘿，有时候你提问时，听起来太幼稚了。” 我当时很惊讶。然后我意识到问题出在哪里——我直白地问：“嘿，你为什么这么做？” 而不是先说明自己的立场，比如“嘿，我注意到……为什么……” 你懂我的意思吗？我没有先展示自己对事情的理解，再提后续问题，而是直接抛出问题，缺乏上下文，让人觉得“嘿，我只是在问个很基础的问题”。所以，这种反馈对我来说特别珍贵。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The feedback you're getting is pretty incredible, like the stuff you shared about someone saying you come across as angry in a meeting if you ask questions or you sound a junior. I don't know if I've ever gotten anyone to give me that brutally honest feedback. When those specific cases, what was it about these people that helped them give you this feedback? Is that what you talked about, you built trust with them over the years or is there something you did to get that kind of feedback?
turns.zh: 你得到的反馈真是令人惊叹，比如有人说你在会议上提问时显得很生气，或者听起来很不成熟。我不知道自己有没有得到过如此直白的反馈。具体来说，这些人是如何帮助你获得这些反馈的？你是和他们建立了信任关系，还是采取了其他措施？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: I mean, it's definitely they trusted me and they cared about me. They trust that if they tell me the feedback without translating, that I would see the intent behind it. And they were able to do that, because after months and years of working together, they know how to respond to feedback. Because what happens is most people, when you have to get feedback, you kind of have to really do a lot of translation work so that it lands, "I don't want to hurt your feeling. I don't want you to take this." I just told people, "You don't have to that with me." That's one. And then the other thing, too, is people reciprocate also how you talk. I'm not saying I talk to people like this, but I try to be vulnerable with people so they know we can be vulnerable and things are safe like, "I really want to hear things the way you experience it."
turns.zh: 我的意思是，他们肯定信任我，也关心我。他们相信即使不翻译反馈，我也能理解其背后的意图。他们能做到这一点，是因为经过数月乃至数年的合作，他们知道如何正确接收反馈。大多数人在获取反馈时，都会过度翻译，比如“我不想伤害你的感情。别往心里去。”而我会告诉人们：“没必要对我这样。” 这是一方面。另一方面，人们也会根据你的沟通方式做出回应。我不是说我自己就这样，但我会努力展现脆弱的一面，让对方知道我们可以坦诚相待，营造安全的氛围，比如“我真的想听你如何体验这件事。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So, there's a lot of foundation setting that you do to create this environment where people are like, "Jules, here's something that's going wrong. You can work on this."
turns.zh: 明白了。所以，你需要做很多基础性的铺垫工作，才能营造出一种让人们觉得“朱尔斯，这里出了点问题，你可以来处理”的氛围。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome takeaway. One other thread I wanted to pull on is you mentioned focusing on strengths and how that ends up being really important. Something I'm a big believer in is focusing on strengths versus trying to make your weaknesses much, much stronger. Is there any advice you can share to better understand what your strengths are, why that's an approach to take in developing your skills?
turns.zh: 这真是很棒的启发。我还想追问一下你提到的专注于自身优势，以及这为何最终变得至关重要。我的一个核心观点是，专注于自身优势比试图把弱点强化的效果要好得多。你能否分享一些建议，帮助我们更好地认识自己的优势，以及为什么在提升技能时应采取这种方法？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: For the strengths, breakthroughs. For me, a lot of it was talking to my mentor, Lawrence Ripsher. And I organized this event for Black PMs at Pinterest, where Lawrence was speaking, and then we were talking about, "Hey, watch should we talk about, et cetera." I don't know how, but in the conversation he talked about doubling down your strengths more than on fixing your weaknesses, and then he used me as an example. Then the fun part is he had this approach of how you actually find your strength. It's a very simple question, where basically he's like, "Hey, what is something that a lot of people say you're good at, but you think it's not a big deal or it's not that important?" And that's the key. I always that's what resonated with me. I was like, "Oh, a lot of people keep saying I'm really good at networking." (00:52:26): I'm like semi-introvert, so I'm like, "Hold on, I don't know." [inaudible 00:52:32] not everyone or people will tell me, "Hey, you have asked great questions." And I'm like, "I asked basic questions." And then he helped me understand, "Actually, that's how you know it's a strength." Now, what you need to figure out is how do you get more out of that strength. An analogy, by the way, is imagine that you saw a fish and you were like, "Hey, you're really good at swimming." And then the fish would be like, "Oh. Duh, doesn't everybody swim?" And so, that's the key and I invite people to think about that question like, "What's something people keep telling you you're good at, but you yourself don't think is a big deal?" And that's how I was able to find a bunch of my strengths. ] (00:53:09): For me, generally I'm thoughtful, ask great questions. I also simplify problems a lot. I mean, we work together on a product sense article, which is a very complex thing, made it more simple. And then once you identify the strength, then it helps to also think about why are you good at this thing? Because that's the underlying resource that you have. A big part for me is I'm actually quite curious. And fun fact, I don't think of myself as curious, but people keep telling me I am. And even my mom was telling me when I was a kid, I used to always try to unscrew toys to see how they work in the inside. That's one thing: being curious help me ask the questions and so on. And then the other thing, too, is once you have the strength, you want to understand the shadow side of it, and that's the connection between your strength and weaknesses. (00:54:02): That was a key breakthrough for me, especially Lawrence helped me understand that. Strengthen and weakness, it's not a binary thing. It's like the same thing, but it's a dial. In some context it's good, in other contexts it's serving you. An example in my cases is... I talked about I ask great questions, but sometimes I ask a question without context, I might come across as less knowledgeable. Or another thing for me is I'm able to take very complex problems and then create a mental model that's much simpler, whether it's growth or other things. But until I come up with that mental model, if I'm in a meeting with you, I won't talk much about that topic. Basically, I'm more quiet than other people when people want to hear my point of view because I'm just listening and trying to create a mental model of the situation. You're seeing how the same strength is perceived as a weakness depending on context. And once you have that... For me, I feel more empowered. I'm like, "Oh, I just have to dial down a little bit here or dial a little bit here," and I also know this thing is serving me, which is why I keep doing the bad side of it.
turns.zh:
谈谈我的优势和突破之处。对我来说，关键在于与导师Lawrence Ripsher的交流。我曾在Pinterest为黑人产品经理组织了一场活动，Lawrence在会上发言，之后我们探讨了：“嘿，我们该聊些什么呢？”我不知道他怎么做到的，但在对话中他提到，要比起改正弱点，更要深挖自身优势。接着他以我为例，讲解如何真正发现自己的长处。这很简单，他会问：“嘿，有什么事大家都说你很擅长，但你自己却不以为然？”这才是关键所在。我深有共鸣。比如别人总说我很擅长社交，但我总觉得这没什么大不了的。而Lawrence让我明白，这恰恰是我的优势所在。关键在于如何深挖这种优势。举个例子，如果你看到一条鱼，你说：“嘿，你游泳真厉害。”鱼可能会说：“哦，这有什么，人都会游泳啊。”这就是区别所在。我鼓励大家思考这个问题：“有什么事大家都说你擅长，但你自己却不以为然？”这就是我发现自己众多优势的方式。

（00:52:26）对我来说，总体来说，我善于思考，能提出好问题。我还善于简化复杂问题。比如我们一起写产品文档时，虽然内容很复杂，但我能让它变得更易懂。一旦识别出优势，就要思考自己为何擅长这件事？因为这正是你内在的资源。对我来说，好奇心很重要。虽说我不觉得自己好奇，但大家总这么说。小时候我妈妈就说，我总爱拆玩具看看里面构造。这就是好奇心帮助我提问的例子。另一方面，优势与劣势并非二元对立，而是同一事物的不同侧面。比如我擅长提问，但有时脱离上下文提问会显得不够专业。又比如我能把复杂问题简化成简单模型，无论是增长策略还是其他领域。但在形成模型前，如果在会议上发言，我会保持沉默，因为我需要先理解全局。同一种优势在不同情境下可能被视为劣势。一旦意识到这一点，我会更有掌控感。我会想：“哦，这里需要调整一点，那里需要调整一点。”同时我也明白这些优势如何为我服务。
究竟为什么我总是一再重蹈覆辙？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. This all often comes back to mentors in your life. I want to get to talking about mentorship and how you find your mentors, how you work with them, all that kind of stuff; something we've been touching on a bunch and I'm excited to begin to. Maybe to start, can you just talk about some of the mentors you've had in your life, some of the most impactful mentors that you've had?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这一切往往都归结于你生命中的导师。我想聊聊导师制度，如何找到自己的导师，以及如何与他们合作等诸多话题；这些内容我们已经多次提及，我很期待能深入探讨。或许先从你人生中遇到的导师说起吧——那些对你影响最深的导师？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: I've definitely had a large number of mentors over the years. Fun fact, when I came to the area eight years ago, I didn't know anyone.
turns.zh: 这些年我确实遇到了很多导师。说个趣事，我八年前刚来到这个地区时，一个人都不认识。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: It took a while to build those relationships. I talked earlier about Bangaly Kaba who sort of helped me figure out how to grow Slack even though he wasn't working outside, but helped me have the frameworks. I talked about Lawrence Ripsher. He helped me discover my strengths and also how to lean into them. Aaron Teague is another friend and mentor who brought me to Google, actually. And there's also Bradley Horowitz, former VP of Google Photos, also helped me in terms of how do you think about leadership and so on. Many other folks, Nikhyl Singhal, VP at Meta helped me with PM career. So, lots of mentors for sure.
turns.zh: 建立这些关系花了不少时间。我之前提到的Bangaly Kaba，虽然他不从事外部工作，但他帮助我理清了如何发展Slack的思路，还提供了框架。我还提到了Lawrence Ripsher，他帮我发现了自己的优势，并教会我如何充分发挥这些优势。Aaron Teague是另一位朋友兼导师，实际上是他把我引荐到了谷歌。还有谷歌相册的前VP Bradley Horowitz，他在领导力等方面的见解对我帮助很大。此外还有Meta的VP Nikhyl Singhal，他在产品管理职业规划方面给了我很多指导。导师可真多啊！

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, that's the killer list. Two questions. One, what do you look for in a mentor when you're trying to find someone to work with? And then two, how do you actually find these people? Most people listening are like, "Wow, I would love an amazing mentor to help me in my career. I don't know how to find one." What advice do you have for folks to finding a mentor?
turns.zh: 好的，这就是一份精彩的名单。我有两个问题：一、在寻找合作导师时，你会关注哪些方面？二、如何实际找到这些导师？大多数听众都会说：“哇，我也想找到一位优秀的导师来助力我的职业发展，但不知道该怎么找。”对此你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: I look for two things. One is, are you good at one specific thing I'm trying to get better at? And then two is, are you good at explaining it? Those two, at least for me, they're important. I know people are really good at their roles, at their job and at the subject, but they don't actually know how they do it or they don't really want to explain or cannot explain easily. So, that's what I look for. And then in terms of where I find these people, it's really everywhere. If you look at the list I mentioned earlier, Bangaly I met at an event. Facebook had a recruiting event, I showed up, I see this guy, I'm like, "Oh. Hi." Chat a little bit. I talked about Lawrence, who's now a close friend. I met Lawrence at a dinner. He organized a dinner for underrepresented PMs, we chatted, one thing led to the other, and then he became a mentor and friend. Bradley was at a fundraiser. And Nikhyl was an intro via email. Somebody was like, "Oh, you should meet Nikhyl." (00:57:41): I know this sounds counterintuitive. I don't think the hard part is where to find them; it's more about finding the right person and then how do you get a foot in? Now, what I've seen... A lot of people, sometimes they get mentors who are too senior or who don't actually think about the topic they're interested in. Maybe they did five years ago, but once you find the right person, the key is like, "How do you have that initial conversation? How do you get the foot in the door?" And what I've found is you should make the smallest ask possible, which is the opposite of what 95% of people do. 95% of people is like, "Hey, I've never met you, but I heard your talk or I saw you on LinkedIn or whatever. Can we set up a call?" (00:58:29): That's like a big ask. What I do... For example, there's this person who came to Slack, he was head of product of a major company and then he gave a talk about different methods to improve products. He had this concept of finding the heat for products. He spoke at the company, I got his email, and I reached out in the evening and I was like, "Hey, thanks so much for speaking today. We talked about finding the heat for products. Is there an example of product that you think was created with this approach?" Something he could answer in literally two minutes via email? That was my question. It wasn't like, "Hey, you talked. Now, I feel entitled to meet with you." But then the key is once you get that foot in the door, it could be a quick email, a tweet, a quick chat at an event, that sort of thing, and you get some advice that's useful, the key is to circle back with them at a later point and show that you've actually made good use of the advice. (00:59:30): I think that's the thing nobody does. What I would do... For example, there's currently the CEO of a top tech company I met an event. She spoke there and then she gave some advice that was useful. I emailed her a follow-up type thing and then she gave me advice about how to rethink the mission statement for my nonprofit, all via email. Then at some point I was like, "Hey, I've applied your problem trend competency framework to crafting the mission for my nonprofit. Here's where we landed. That was super helpful. Thank you so much." Replies back. And then what I would do then later is maybe a month later or two months, X months later, I can reach out again for another problem and maybe I could say, "Hey, this time it's a little bit more nuanced. Can we grab 15 minutes?" And the person was like, "Yeah, sure." That person was very, very busy. I was like, "Hey, let's do it." And then over time we become Facebook friends, that sort of thing, but that's the approach I take.
turns.zh:
我寻找两个关键点。第一，你是否擅长我正努力提升的某项技能？第二，你是否善于把它解释清楚？至少对我而言，这两点至关重要。我知道有些人确实在自己的领域、工作或专业上非常出色，但他们并不真正了解自己是如何做到的，或者不愿意或无法轻易解释清楚。所以这就是我所看重的。至于如何找到这些人才，答案其实无处不在。拿我之前提到的班加利来说，我是在一场活动上认识他的。Facebook举办了一场招聘会，现场遇见了他。我跟他聊了几句，还提到了现在是我的好友的劳伦斯。当时我在一场晚宴上认识了劳伦斯，他为那些代表性不足的产品经理组织了一次聚会，我们聊得投机，后来他成了我的导师和朋友。布拉德利是在一场募捐活动上结识的。尼基尔则是通过邮件介绍认识的。有人说：“哦，你应该认识尼基尔。”（00:57:41）：我知道这听起来有点反常。我觉得关键不在于如何找到他们，而在于找到合适的人之后，如何迈出第一步。我的经验是……很多人找的导师要么职位太高，要么对自己感兴趣的领域缺乏深入思考。也许他们五年前曾研究过某个主题，但一旦找到对的人，关键在于如何开启对话？如何打开局面？我的做法是……比如，有个来Slack的人，是某大公司的产品负责人，曾做过关于产品改进方法的演讲。他提到了“寻找产品热点”的概念。他在公司演讲后，我拿到了他的邮箱，当晚就发邮件说：“嘿，感谢你的演讲。我们聊到如何寻找产品热点。你能举个用这个方法打造产品的例子吗？”这不过是两个字的问题。不是那种自以为高高在上的请求。而是关键在于一旦打开局面，可以发个简短的邮件、发个推特、在活动上简单聊聊之类的，获取有用的建议后，再适时回访，展示自己切实应用了这些建议。（00:59:30）：我觉得这才是大多数人忽视的。比如，我在一次活动上认识了某家顶尖科技公司的CEO。她在会上分享了有用的建议。我发了后续邮件，她就给了我关于如何重新构思非营利组织使命宣言的建议，全程通过邮件沟通。后来我又发邮件说，“嘿，我把你的问题导向能力框架应用到了非营利组织的使命制定中，我们得出了这些结论，非常有帮助。谢谢。”她回复了。然后大约一个月或两个月、几个月后，我再联系她，提出另一个问题，可能说：“嘿，这次问题更复杂些，能抽出15分钟吗？”她答应了。当时她非常忙。我就说：“好啊，那就见一面吧。”随着时间推移，我们逐渐建立了联系。
成为Facebook好友之类的，但这就是我的处事方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a good advice. It reminds me of Tim Ferris's advice also, which is just like, "Don't go up to someone and be like, 'Will you be my mentor?'" Everyone's going to be like, "I don't have time for that." Instead, to your point, it's the exact opposite. Just start asking simple questions and then over time build up relationship, and then over time, maybe you start meeting regularly. But don't start big; start small.
turns.zh: 这真是个好建议。这让我想起蒂姆·费里斯（Tim Ferris）的建议，他曾说过：“别直接走上前去问别人‘你能做我的导师吗？’” 大家都会觉得：“我可没时间应付这种事。”相反，正如你所说，方法恰恰相反。先从简单的问题入手，然后逐渐建立关系，随着时间推移，或许就能开始定期会面。但别一开始就把目标定得太高，要从小处着手。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: You. As small as possible.
turns.zh: 你要尽可能保持低调。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's not like you just have one mentor. You've listed a whole bunch of people that have helped you over your career. It's not like, "Here's the person, they have to be perfect." It sounds like you kind of identify, "Here's a skill or an area I want to focus and this person is going to be really good at that."
turns.zh: 你不只是有一个导师吧。你列举了职业生涯中帮助过你的许多人。并不是说非得找个完美的人才行。听起来你更倾向于这样：先明确自己想专注的技能或领域，然后找到在这方面很擅长的人。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Then I also just love the point about it feels really hard to find an amazing mentor. From what I'm hearing, the main thing you do is just go to things, attend events, basically go events, meet people, right? That's kind of the foundation in which you're sharing is just meet as many people as you can, and amongst that group, you'll find people that are probably going to be helpful.
turns.zh: 我还很欣赏你提到要找到优秀导师其实挺难这点儿。照你说的方法，主要就是多参加活动，结识新朋友，对吧？这就是你分享的核心理念——尽可能多地结交人脉，然后从中筛选出能提供帮助的人。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah. And I understand it can be harder for some folks. I mean, now I have two young kids, so I don't do as many events. I've also met quite a few people through introductions, sometimes being cold outreach. I had a chat with Shishir through cold outreach [inaudible 01:01:44] a very clear question, and then he offered to come to Black PMs and share some insights. Those kinds of things happen, too, but you have to show the person that you're going to make really good use of their time. You have to give really specific contexts like, "Hey, let's grab coffee." It's like, "Hey, here's a very specific question. Can you share some thoughts or point via email?" And then they might offer, "Hey, why don't we just talk?" That sort of thing, too. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。我理解对有些人来说确实更难。比如我现在有两个年幼的孩子，所以参加活动的机会少了。不过我也通过介绍结识了不少人，偶尔也会主动联系。比如我通过主动联系认识了希希尔（Shishir）[未录音 01:01:44]，提出一个很明确的问题，然后他就主动提议来Black PMs分享见解。这类情况也会发生，但你得让对方觉得自己的时间花得值。要给出具体场景，比如“我们一起喝杯咖啡吧”，或者“我有个很具体的问题，想请教一下”之类的。然后对方可能会说：“那我们直接聊聊吧”。这种方式也很有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That works really well. Anytime I get an email request of, "Hey, could we do a 15-minute Zoom or a copy chat," I quickly do not have time for that. But an actual question that I can be really helpful with really quickly, that's so much easier, so that makes a lot of sense. The next thing I wanted to ask you is: how do you build and continue this relationship? And then once you actually start engaging regularly, what do you suggest folks talk about in these meetings if they're ongoing.
turns.zh: 这方法确实很有效。每次收到“能不能用15分钟的Zoom或文档聊天”的邮件请求时，我都会很快回复没空。但如果是能快速提供帮助的具体问题，就容易多了。所以这点很明智。接下来我想问：如何建立并维系这种关系？等定期交流开始后，如果会面持续下去，你建议大家在会上聊些什么？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: I make sure to bring something very specific that I'm dealing with where they can provide input. And this is the opposite of what many people do where they're like, "Hey, can you tell me about how you... Whatever, your path to PM," which may or may not be relevant to them, versus, "Hey, I've interviewed for three companies. I'm trying to decide among those three. Can I walk you through my thought process and get your feedback?" So, it's very different. I definitely make sure I bring a very specific context, and sometime it could be... I mentioned the example of Bangali like, "Hey, I'm now a growth PM at Slack. I'm trying to improve activation. Can I talk to you about how you approach growth in general?" Or it could be, "Hey, I'm having internal..." Let's say I have internal mentors at Google and I have a few, then it's like, "Hey, I'm about to have this negotiation with this team. Can I walk you through my thought process and hear your advice?" So, it's very specific things. (01:03:37): And then the other thing I'll say, too, is when I talk to mentors, I always take notes. I mean, I'm seeing you even here in this interview. You're taking notes. These are basic things people don't actually think about it sometimes. And then when I follow up, whether it's via email or in person, I bring up older conversations. It's like, "Hey, remember last time we told about X? I did it," or "Hey, how's your daughter? I know she was going to college this semester. How did that go?" So, it always feels like a continuation of a conversation and it feels like an actual relationship instead of transactional interactions. And then the other thing, too, is I try really hard to identify ways that I can be helpful. Sometimes, at the end of chat I'll be like, "Hey, is there anything I can help you with? Anything top of mind for you?" And sometimes the person could be senior or wealthy, doesn't matter, and they're like, "Actually, yes. I'd love to better understand how the team is really doing. Nobody will tell me the truth," or "Hey, I am trying to hire for this role. You have [inaudible 01:04:43] Black PMs. Do you mind sharing?" There's always ways you can help, but most people are so focused on themselves that they miss out on these opportunities.
turns.zh:
我一定会带去一些我正在处理的具体问题，让对方能给出建议。这和很多人做事的思路正好相反——很多人会说：“嘿，能不能跟我讲讲你如何成为产品经理的？”但这对对方未必有用。而我会说：“嘿，我面试了三家公司，现在要在它们之间做选择。能不能跟你分享一下我的思考过程，听听你的建议？”这样才更有针对性。比如，我曾和Bangali聊天，提到自己现在是Slack的增长产品经理，正在提升用户激活率，问对方如何看待增长策略。又比如，我在谷歌有内部导师，遇到难题时会说：“嘿，我马上要和这个团队谈判，能不能回顾一下我们之前的对话？”这些都是具体的案例。

（01:03:37）另外，我要强调的是，和导师交流时一定要做好笔记。看看你现在在采访中也是这样，不断记录笔记。这些基本的细节人们有时会忽视。之后无论是邮件沟通还是当面跟进，我都会提起之前的对话。比如：“嘿，还记得上次我们讨论X的事情吗？我已经做了。”或者“你女儿怎么样了？我知道她这学期上大学了，进展如何？”这样交流就延续了之前的对话，让关系更真实而非交易式互动。

还有，我会尽力找到能提供帮助的切入点。比如结束对话时会问：“有没有什么地方我能帮到你？你现在最关心什么？” 有时对方是高管或富有人士，但他们也会说：“其实有啊，我想更清楚团队的真实情况，但没人肯跟我说实话。” 或者：“嘿，我想招人填这个职位，你手下有黑人产品经理吗？能分享一下吗？” 总有帮助的机会，但大多数人太专注于自己，错过了这些机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The point about coming back to the person and sharing what impact their advice had and how it went is so good, because to your point, it just feels like you're sharing all this advice and just isn't going anywhere. And then note-taking, such great stuff. This is really good advice. I could see how it would work on me if someone's asking me for advice.
turns.zh: 关于回头分享建议效果的部分很棒，因为正如你所说，光是分享建议却没效果的感觉很糟糕。还有记笔记，这真是好建议。如果有人向我寻求建议，我能想象这方法对我的效果。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: By the way, I mean we didn't know each other two years ago, right?
turns.zh: 对了，我们两年前还不认识，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's right.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah. It's like a similar process, where we got to know each other mostly via email and led to the other, and we try to help each other.
turns.zh: 是啊。这过程很相似，我们主要通过邮件了解彼此，然后逐渐深入，互相帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And look at us now. Any final thoughts before we wrap up and head to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 看看我们现在。最后总结一下再进入激动人心的闪电问答环节，有什么想法吗？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: I have found the process of learning how to be a PM very difficult and I also find it quite rewarding. And I want to set expectation, especially for people who are early in their career, people may be frustrated by the process, because you have all these skills. We listed, I don't know, half a dozen, a dozen that you want to get better at. So, be patient. Then also it takes a while to see massive differences, but once you see those differences, you set yourself apart from your peers. That's one thing. And then the other thing, too, is it's really building muscles more so for the EQ stuff, but even for the IQ stuff. You have to practice. It's not just read Lenny's top 10 articles for two hours and then you're good. Read them, do what they say, get feedback after you do what they say and say like, "Huh, it worked for me. It didn't work for me." Reread them again, find mentors, et cetera. It's a long process and I don't think people have that mental model around how to learn in general, but also specifically how to learn the PM skills.
turns.zh:
我发现学习如何成为一名产品经理的过程非常困难，但也收获颇丰。我想先设定一下预期——尤其是对职业生涯早期的人而言，你们可能会对这个过程感到沮丧，因为要掌握的技能实在太多。我们列出了一堆想要提升的技能，比如社交商、智商提升等等，但这些都需要长期努力才能见成效。一旦你看到进步，就会从同行中脱颖而出。这是第一点。

另外，要想真正提升技能，特别是社交商方面，还需要不断练习。比如，读完莱尼的十大文章后，不能只停留在理解层面，而是要付诸实践。完成后反思效果，调整方法，再次总结。整个过程漫长且艰辛，我认为人们对学习的认知存在误区，更别说学习产品经理技能了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I imagine there's also this one step forward, two step back experience that often happens, too, where you're just like, "Oh, I thought I figured out how to think about strategy, and this one failed." And you're like, "Oh, that was useless." No, this is how you learn. You fail sometimes. Oftentimes, it works out slowly but surely you move forward.
turns.zh: 我相信大家也经历过那种一日千里的进步与反复退步的循环。比如你以为自己掌握了战略思维，结果却失败了。然后又会说：“这根本没用。”但这就是学习的过程。失败不可避免，但只要坚持，总会取得进步。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah, totally.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Well, with that, we have reached our very exciting lightning round. Since we've gone a little long, I'm going to keep it just four questions. I'm just going to go through them pretty fast, whatever comes to mind. Fire off. You ready?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，接下来是激动人心的闪电问答环节。由于时间有点紧张，我只准备了四个问题，会尽快提问。大家随意准备，准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你向他人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.en: One of them is Never Split the Difference by Chris Voss. It's about negotiations. There's actually also a masterclass on it.
turns.zh: 其中一本是克里斯·沃斯的《永不妥协的谈判》。主要讲谈判技巧。实际上还有相关大师课。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was just going to say that. I watched that. That was really good.
turns.zh: 我刚想说这个。我看过那门课，确实很棒。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. And then another one is Connect by Carole Robin. It's inspired by Stanford's Touchy-Feely class, if you've ever heard of it.
turns.zh: 是的。另一本是卡罗尔·罗宾的《连接》。灵感来自斯坦福大学的“触觉感知”课程，如果你听说过的话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. She did a guest post for the newsletter, actually.
turns.zh: 对。她确实为我们的通讯写过一篇客座文章。

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Oh, really? Awesome. Yeah. It's really a helpful especially as you are thinking about the EQ skills and how to improve your relationships with people.
turns.zh: 哦，真的吗？太棒了。确实有助于提升情商，改善人际关系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I highly recommend that book. I haven't read it, but I read a lot of things about the class and my friends have been in that class and she wrote this guest post. That sounds like a really good pick for EQ, so I'm actually going to re-pick it up. Next question: favorite other podcast that isn't this podcast.
turns.zh: 太好了。我强烈推荐那本书。虽然我没读过，但读过很多关于这门课的介绍，我的朋友们上过那门课，她还写了客座文章。这对提升情商来说确实是个不错的选择，我打算重新翻出来看看。下一个问题：除了我们自己的播客，你最喜欢的其他播客是什么？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: Lex Fridman is one I'll call out. Brings really interesting speakers and also on diverse topics, so I find it really helpful.
turns.zh: 我要特别推荐莱克斯·弗里德曼的播客。他邀请的嘉宾非常有趣，话题也很广泛，我觉得很受益。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I also love that podcast. Favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我也超爱那个播客。最近最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: I watch fewer now. Top Gun: Maverick is a movie I really like. I'm sure many people have seen it. For me, it's like just going back in the 80s. And then TV show is Never Have I Ever. It's coming of age in America, Indian teenager. Pretty funny and also deep.
turns.zh: 我现在看得比较少了。《壮志凌云：独行侠》是一部我非常喜欢的电影。我相信很多人都看过。对我来说，这部电影就像是带我回到了80年代。还有一部电视剧叫《我从未做过的事》。这部剧讲述了美国和印度青少年的成长故事，既有趣又深刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I haven't heard of that one. We'll check it out. Final question: favorite interview question that you like to ask folks when you're interviewing them?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我没听说过这部剧。我们会去看看的。最后一个问题：你在面试别人时，最喜欢问他们哪类问题？

turns.speaker: Jules Walter
turns.en: One I used to ask a lot is: what's something work related that you're trying to get better at? Sometimes I change the wording of it, but a big part of it is trying to understand how self-aware people are, to which extent they have a growth mindset, and then also how honest and vulnerable they can be. What I will say, though, about interview question, by the way, is I don't anchor a lot on the first question. What I find the most value from are the follow-ups. Once you ask that question, you can take in various directions like, "Why did you focus on this versus other things? How did this come to your attention? Was it feedback you sought or feedback people gave you, et cetera?" Yeah.
turns.zh: 我以前经常问的一个问题是：“在工作方面，你正在努力提升哪方面的能力？”有时我会调整措辞，但核心在于了解应聘者对自身的认知程度、他们的成长型思维模式，以及他们能多坦诚和脆弱。顺便说一句，关于面试问题，我不会太依赖第一个问题。对我来说，后续提问更有价值。一旦你提出第一个问题，就可以朝多个方向深入，比如：“你为什么会专注于这个领域而非其他领域？这个问题是如何引起你注意的？这是你主动寻求的反馈还是别人给你的反馈？”是的。

turns.en: Awesome advice. Jules, this interview was a longtime coming. It was everything I hoped it would be and more. Thank you again so much for being here. Two final questions: where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and learn more, and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 很棒的建议。朱尔斯，这次采访期待已久了。它完全符合我的期待，甚至超出预期。再次感谢你能来参加采访。最后两个问题：如果听众想了解更多信息，如何在网上找到你？听众又能如何为你提供帮助？

turns.en: In terms of finding me, Twitter is one place to start. My handle is @julesdwalt. And then in terms of how people can be useful, it's really about paying it forward and then sharing this with others, especially parts that people find useful.
turns.zh: 想找到我，可以从Twitter开始。我的账号是@julesdwalt。至于听众如何提供帮助，主要就是传递正能量，并与他人分享有用的内容，尤其是那些对他人有帮助的部分。

turns.en: Amazing. Jules, thank you so much. We'll chat again soon.
